caption:
I went there hoping to inspire a room full of hospitality people. I left feeling pretty damn inspired myself🧡

Last week, I had the privilege of speaking at Balancing Plates in McLaren Vale. An event created by people in hospitality, FOR people in hospitality. And it sold out weeks before the night even arrived.

Whenever I speak, my goal is pretty simple. I want people to walk away with something they can put into practice tomorrow, without spending a single dollar. But more than that, I want them to feel excited about what they do.

And this room? They blew me away.

The honesty. The openness. The genuine sense of community. And most importantly, the willingness to make things BETTER.

Because let’s face it, we can sit around and complain about this industry all fucking day. Or we can have the conversations that actually move us forward.

That’s what I saw in that room.

People who care deeply about their industry, their teams, and the future of hospitality.

And when we take better care of ourselves and our people, our guests feel the difference too.

A massive thank you to the Balancing Plates team, the incredible sponsors who made the evening possible, and everyone who showed up and contributed.

This industry has some pretty extraordinary people in it. And nights like this remind me exactly why I love being part of it.

caption:
I’m a sucker for a restaurant that knows how to make you feel fucking special without making a big production out of it.👏

Here are 7 oddly specific things that win me over.

1. When the bartender gives you THAT look.

Your glass is nearly empty, they catch your eye, give you a little nod, and another cocktail is on its way. No waving your arms around like you’re directing traffic.

2. When a server tells you NOT to order something.

“I think you’ve ordered enough food.”

You’re telling me you care more about my experience than squeezing another $28 out of me? Marry me.

3. When the staff have just the right amount of cheek.

A perfectly timed sarcastic comment that has the whole table losing it? I fucking LOVE those people. Give me personality over a rehearsed script any day.

4. When someone is borderline OBSESSED with something on the menu.

Not “Everything’s really good.” I want the server who practically grabs my arm because I haven’t ordered their favourite wine. THAT energy.

5. When someone acknowledges a celebration without making it weird.

A quiet congratulations. A little surprise from the kitchen. Not six staff members clapping while I contemplate crawling under the table.

6. When the outdoor tables aren’t treated like forgotten children.

I’m enjoying a cocktail, not participating in a survival challenge. I shouldn’t need to send a search party inside to order another drink. 😂

7. When someone remembers something random from my last visit.

Not my drink order. The holiday I was planning. The dog I mentioned three weeks ago. That shit gets me EVERY time.

It’s people paying attention, having a personality, and genuinely enjoying making someone else’s day better.

Those are the restaurants I fall in love with🧡

Now tell me yours. What’s one oddly specific thing a restaurant does that wins you over?

caption:
I’ve spent more than 20 years in hospitality, and sitting at a bar is still one of my favourite places to watch great hospitality happen.

Here are 7 things I notice almost immediately:

1. The acknowledgement. 
Even when they’re slammed, does someone make eye contact or give me a quick nod?

2. How they treat newcomers. 
Are the regulars getting all the attention, or does everyone feel welcome?

3. The menu. 
Is someone offering one, or am I left hunting for it?

4. Their awareness. 
Are they watching the entire bar, or just focused on making drinks?

5. Their recommendations. 
Do they ask what I enjoy before suggesting something?

6. The solo guest. 
Does someone sitting alone feel just as welcome as a group of six?

7. The goodbye. 
Does anyone notice when a guest leaves?

None of these things requires a fancy cocktail menu or an expensive fit-out.
Just people who genuinely understand hospitality.

alt: Video by Hospitality Advisor ┃Alexis Guttridge on October 30, 2026. May be an image of one or more people, drink and text.

caption:
One of the biggest mistakes I see in restaurants? Trying to fix the problem you can see without understanding what’s causing it.

Here are a few examples of where I’d look first.

1. Staff keep leaving.
Before blaming the hiring market, I’d want to know who they’re working for, how they’re being managed, and what their first 30 days actually look like.

2. Service is inconsistent.
Before scheduling another training session, I’d look at what happens before the doors open. Are expectations clear? Is there a proper pre-shift? Does anyone follow up on what was taught yesterday?

3. Managers are burning out.
Before telling them to delegate more, I’d want to know what decisions they’re actually allowed to make. Are they empowered to lead, or does everything still have to go through the owner?

4. Guests aren’t coming back.
Before changing the menu or offering discounts, I’d look at the entire guest experience. What happens when they arrive? How do they feel when they leave? And does anyone follow up after their visit?

5. The owner can’t step away.
Before hiring another manager, I’d want to understand why the restaurant still depends on one person to make every decision.

Here’s the thing.

Sometimes the problem everyone is talking about isn’t actually the problem.

It’s just the symptom.

And if you keep fixing symptoms, you’re going to keep having the same fucking conversations six months from now 🤷‍♀️

alt: Video by Hospitality Advisor ┃Alexis Guttridge on October 31, 2026. May be an image of magazine and text.

caption:
Some of the best hospitality improvements I’ve seen haven’t cost a restaurant a single dollar.

And this is something I talk about A LOT when I’m working with hospitality teams.

We often assume that improving the guest experience means investing in something new. New systems, more staff, better technology or another training program.

But sometimes the biggest opportunity is simply becoming more AWARE of what’s already happening around you.

Here’s what I mean.

1. Pay attention to your team’s natural strengths.

You’ve probably got someone on your team who’s brilliant at making nervous guests feel comfortable. Someone else who can read a room without saying a word. Or someone who has an incredible ability to make new staff feel welcome.

Are you recognising those strengths? Are you helping those people develop them? Are you encouraging them to share what they do naturally with the rest of the team?

2. Get specific about what great hospitality looks like.

Telling your team to “give great service” isn’t training. Talk about the little moments. How you acknowledge someone when you’re busy. How you recognise when a guest needs help without waiting to be asked. How you make someone feel comfortable when they walk through the door.

Give people something they can actually put into practice.

3. Create opportunities for your team to contribute.

Some of the best ideas come from the people doing the work every day. Ask questions, listen to their answers and give them the confidence to suggest a better way of doing something.

Because improving hospitality doesn’t always require a bigger budget. Sometimes it requires better awareness, more intentional leadership and recognising the potential that’s already sitting right in front of you.

And THAT is where some pretty incredible things can happen😉

And if they can’t, is there an easy way to get the information you need? I understand restaurants get busy, but trying to give someone your business shouldn’t feel like hard work.

2. Does their Instagram match the restaurant you walk into?

I’m not talking about whether the photos are beautiful. Does the personality, the atmosphere, the experience they’ve been showing you actually exist when you arrive? Or does it feel like you’ve walked into a completely different restaurant?

3. What happens in the first 30 seconds?

Does somebody acknowledge you, even if they’re busy? Do you feel like they’re genuinely happy you’ve arrived, or like you’ve just interrupted something? That first interaction can set the tone for the entire night.

4. How does the team interact with each other?

I’m ALWAYS watching this. Are they smiling, communicating, helping each other? Or does everybody look like they’re just trying to survive the shift? You can feel the difference, and it tells me a lot about what’s happening behind the scenes.

5. Does anyone seem genuinely excited about what’s happening in the restaurant?

Maybe it’s a new dish, a wine they’re loving, or just the fact that it’s a busy Friday night. I love walking into a restaurant where the team actually seems proud of the place they work.

6. What does the room feel like before you even sit down?

Is there energy? Is the music right? Is the lighting comfortable? Does the restaurant feel like someone has actually thought about how it feels to be there, not just how it looks?

And the funny thing is, I haven’t even ordered a fucking drink yet. 😂

None of these things can tell me whether the food will be good. But they tell me an awful lot about the people, the culture, and how much thought has gone into the guest experience.

Don’t just assume they’ll figure everything else out because they’re great with people.

Give them opportunities to build their confidence. Let them lead a pre-shift, recommend a wine they’re excited about, or take ownership of a guest experience.

And when they do something brilliantly? Tell them WHAT they did well and WHY it mattered.

Most importantly, give them room to make mistakes, ask questions, and grow.

Natural talent is a wonderful thing.

But what you do with that talent as a leader can make all the difference.

alt: Video by Hospitality Advisor ┃Alexis Guttridge on October 05, 2026. May be a meme of food and text.

caption:
I think owning a restaurant can really fuck with your sense of what being a good owner is supposed to look like.

You care more than anyone. You probably know more about the business than anyone. And when you’ve spent years being the person who fixes things, answers the questions and steps in when something goes wrong, it’s very easy to start believing that being needed is part of the job.

I definitely did.

But some of the restaurant owners I respect most are still incredibly involved in their businesses. They haven’t stopped caring about the details or lowered their standards. They’ve just figured out where they’re actually needed and, maybe more importantly, where they’re not.

They hire good people and let them be good. They let managers make decisions. They can hear something they don’t agree with without immediately shutting it down. And when the same problem keeps happening, they’re willing to ask whether they might be contributing to it too.

I think there’s a huge difference between building a restaurant around you and building a restaurant that can thrive because of what you built.

The second one is a hell of a lot harder. But it might also let you take a fucking day off.

alt: Video by Hospitality Advisor ┃Alexis Guttridge on October 01, 2026. May be an image of one or more people, people smiling and text.

caption:
It’s usually the little things you remember most — and the little things that keep you coming back.

1. Somewhere to put the thing you’re awkwardly holding.

A bag, coat, umbrella, flowers, shopping. They notice you trying to solve the problem before you end up putting it on the floor or balancing it on the back of your chair.

2. A minute to actually settle in.

You’ve just walked in, taken off your coat, moved your bag, pulled out your chair. Great service reads the moment instead of immediately launching into water, specials and “Have you dined with us before?”

3. What you’ll need for the food before you need it.

The shell bowl with the prawns. Extra napkins with the ribs. A steak knife before the steak. The restaurant knows how its food is eaten. You shouldn’t have to ask.

4. Room for what’s coming next.

Don’t arrive with three dishes and then watch the guests play fucking Tetris with their own table. Great teams make the space before they need it.

5. To repeat something the restaurant already knows.

The allergy in the booking notes. The anniversary mentioned at the door. The fact that someone needs to leave by eight. Great restaurants make information travel with the guest.

6. Permission for your table to have its own pace.

Some tables want to linger. Some have theatre tickets. Some want another bottle. Some are fucking exhausted and want dessert and the bill. Great service doesn’t force every table through the exact same rhythm.

7. To be rescued from an awkward moment.

You drop your fork. Spill your drink. Mispronounce something on the menu. Walk towards the wrong door. Don’t make a guest feel stupid for needing help.

caption:
There are tiny things that tell me almost immediately I’m in a restaurant that knows what it’s doing.

1. You’re standing at the door and someone carrying three plates still catches your eye and gives you the “we see you” nod on the way past.

2. A glass breaks and nobody reacts except the two people closest to it. One grabs a broom, the other quietly redirects people around it, and the restaurant keeps moving.

3. A table gets up to leave and someone who never served them still looks up and says goodbye.

4. Four tables get seated almost at once and instead of everyone suddenly moving faster, someone quietly starts helping someone else’s section.

5. Two staff members make eye contact from opposite sides of the room and somehow a problem gets fixed without either of them saying a word.

6. A server approaches your table, sees you’re mid-story and does a tiny lap instead of interrupting you just because they’re ready.

7. Someone notices you looking around for something and starts heading toward you before you’ve even put your hand up.

That’s the stuff I notice.

None of it is flashy. Most guests probably couldn’t even tell you it happened.

But when a restaurant really knows what it’s doing, you don’t spend the night trying to get its attention.

It already has yours.

What’s an oddly specific one you’d add?

caption:
One of the hardest things I had to learn in restaurants was not to let one person take up more space in my head than they deserved.

Because they will.

Someone will be rude. Someone will make a completely unreasonable complaint. Someone will talk to you like you’re an idiot when you’ve spent the last six hours handling absolute chaos without blinking.

Sometimes they’re just an asshole. But sometimes they’re having a really shitty day, or going through something you know absolutely nothing about.

Either way, you can’t carry them into the next table.

Deal with what’s in front of you. Fix what you can. Learn from it if there’s something worth learning. Then let it go and give the next guest the same version of you they would’ve gotten before it happened.

I definitely wasn’t always good at that. But after 20+ years in restaurants, I think learning not to let one difficult person change how you show up for everyone else might be one of the most important skills hospitality teaches you.

caption:
I don’t start with what needs fixing. I start with what I can learn.

Before I give a restaurant any advice, I want to understand as much as I can before I influence what I’m seeing.

1. I try to experience everything a guest does before they arrive. I call the restaurant. I try the booking system. I check Google, the website, Instagram. Does anyone answer the phone? Can I actually find the information I need? Does what they’re promising online match what I’m about to experience in person?

2. I go looking for patterns, not complaints. I read reviews, tagged posts and comments. I don’t care that Karen hated her steak. I care when six different people, over six months, describe the same tiny frustration in six different ways. That’s not a bad review anymore. That’s a pattern.

3. I ask people who have absolutely nothing to do with the restaurant. I’ll reach out to people in the hospitality community and ask what they’ve heard or experienced. If I know someone in that city, I may even pay for them to go have dinner and tell me what they noticed. I don’t only want hospitality eyes on a restaurant. I want to know what it feels like to an actual guest.

4. Whenever I can, I have a sneaky dinner myself. I don’t announce who I am. I don’t want special treatment. I want to see the restaurant on a completely ordinary night when nobody has any reason to perform differently because I’m there.

5. Then I start looking upstream. Slow service doesn’t automatically mean a slow server. Someone who can’t answer a menu question isn’t automatically a bad employee. A frantic team doesn’t automatically mean they’re understaffed.

I want to know why.

What happened before service? How were they trained? Who are they waiting for permission from? Is the system helping them or are they fighting it every night?

Because sometimes the thing a guest experiences at 8:15pm started in a management meeting three months ago.

I do a lot of homework before I give a restaurant advice.

Not because I’m trying to catch anyone doing something wrong.

caption:
The longer you’ve owned it, the harder it can be to actually SEE it.

So how do you get fresh eyes on a restaurant you’ve walked into 10,000 times?

A few things I’d try:

Ask another restaurant owner.
Not for a formal audit. Buy them a coffee, walk them through your space and ask: What am I not seeing anymore?

Go somewhere completely different from yours.
Different price point. Different style. Different city if you can. Pay attention to what makes you think, shit, that’s good.

Follow businesses that aren’t your competition.
Sometimes the best ideas come from a winery, hotel, café or restaurant doing something completely different from you.

Go back to something that inspired you in the beginning.
Pick up Setting the Table again. Listen to an old hospitality podcast. Revisit the restaurant that originally made you want to do this.

Ask your team.
They’re seeing things every day that you’re probably not. Ask them one simple question: If this were your restaurant, what’s one thing you’d change?

And yes, sometimes you bring in someone like me.

But the point isn’t WHO gives you the perspective.

The point is making sure you’re still looking for it.

WHAT’S LEFT⁉️

• The way someone greeted you like they were genuinely happy you walked in.

• The table they somehow knew you’d love.

• The server who made you laugh and stopped feeling like a stranger halfway through dinner.

• The tiny thing you mentioned once that someone remembered later.

• The mistake they handled so well it somehow made you like the restaurant even more.

• The feeling that you could stay for another drink without someone silently wishing you’d leave.

• The person who noticed you looking around and helped before you ever had to ask.

• The recommendation you never would’ve ordered yourself and still talk about.

• The moment someone went slightly off-script because it was the right thing to do.

• The regular at the bar who somehow made you feel like a regular too.

• The goodbye that felt just as genuine as the hello.

Great food matters. Of course it does.

But when I think about the restaurants I’ve never forgotten, I remember so much more than what was on the plate.

I remember how it felt to be there.

caption:
Okay Alexis, but what the f*ck am I supposed to change?

Start by looking at the empty seats.

Not all of them. Pick one problem.

Tuesday nights are dead?
Don’t immediately discount. Ask what would give your existing guests a reason to come on a Tuesday.

People love you but only come for special occasions?
Maybe you don’t need to change what you already do well. Could you create another experience, price point or time of day that gives them another reason to use you?

Your regulars aren’t coming as often?
Talk to them. Seriously. Five conversations with people who already love your restaurant might teach you more than another month staring at your bookings.

Something you’ve always done isn’t working anymore?
Stop protecting it because it used to work.

The economy is real. Cost pressures are real. People changing how they spend is real.

But none of those things are reasons to stop experimenting.

You don’t need 15 new ideas. You need to know where to look first.

That’s why I created a free tool that walks you through the same areas I look at when assessing a hospitality business — so you can start spotting the gaps and opportunities yourself.

caption:
Okay, so how did I actually get better at running pre-shift?

A few things that helped me:

1. Don’t make the whole thing about what went wrong yesterday.
If every lineup is just a list of mistakes, your team will start tuning you out. Give feedback, absolutely. But give them something to feel good about too.

2. Teach ONE thing.
A dish. A wine. How you want a guest greeted. A question you want servers asking tonight. They don’t need 14 lessons before service — give them one thing they’ll actually remember.

3. Your energy goes first.
The energy you bring into lineup sets the tone. If you walk in flat, distracted or pissed off, don’t be surprised when that’s what you get back.

Think game day. The best coaches don’t walk into the room five minutes before the game and suck the life out of everyone. They get people switched on.

That doesn’t mean you need to put on some fake rah-rah performance. But if you’re having a shit day and genuinely can’t bring the energy, maybe someone else should run lineup that day.

And one I’d add now after 20+ years in hospitality: don’t wing it.

Take five minutes beforehand and decide what you actually want your team to walk away knowing, feeling or doing differently.

Running a great pre-shift is a skill.
And like I said in the reel — skills can be learned.

🛟Save this for your next lineup.

caption:
Apparently, we have a lot of feelings about restaurant regulars.

My first list about them became one of my most watched reels ever, so here are 17 more things I notice when regulars walk in…

1. Someone usually spots them before they’ve even made it through the door.

2. Their drink sometimes starts being made before they’ve ordered it.

3. They have a favourite seat, and somehow everyone knows which one it is.

4. They know who got promoted, who just got back from holiday and who’s having a rough week.

5. When they bring someone new, they become the unofficial tour guide. “You HAVE to order this.”

6. They notice new staff—and the good ones introduce themselves instead of expecting to be recognised.

7. Another regular gives them that little nod, even though they know nothing about each other outside the restaurant.

8. They know when the team is slammed and somehow become easier guests because of it.

9. They notice everything. New menu. Different glassware. A table moved six inches.

10. They know when their favourite server isn’t quite themselves that night.

11. They often have something they order that isn’t technically on the menu anymore… but someone still makes it.

12. They know which nights are quiet, which are chaos and exactly when they like to come in.

13. Sometimes they know the restaurant’s history better than half the current team.

14. When the restaurant is absolutely packed, they’re genuinely happy for you.

15. They recommend the restaurant like they have shares in the place.

16. Eventually you forget when they became a regular. They’ve just… always been there.

17. Years later, you might not remember what they ordered—but you remember their name, their face and how it felt when they walked through the door.

At some point, great regulars stop feeling like customers.

They become part of the restaurant.

caption:
I spent years watching couples across restaurant tables…

you start to notice things ↓

And no, I’m no relationship therapist here.
This is just what 20+ years of owning and operating restaurants taught me about people.

1. Their knees point toward each other instead of away from each other. Couples deeply into each other physically lean inward without realizing it.

2. One person reaches for their phone every time silence hits. Usually because they’re uncomfortable with real connection or conversation.

3. They thank the staff together instead of separately. Happy couples tend to move through the world more like a team.

4. One person orders for the other without checking first. Sometimes it’s familiarity. Sometimes it’s control. You can usually feel the difference immediately.

5. They still lean in when the other person talks. Even after years together, genuinely connected couples stay curious about each other.

6. One person carries the emotional energy of the entire table. You can feel when one person is trying hard to hold the relationship together.

7. Happy couples usually feel lighter around each other. Not performative. Not exhausting. Just safe, easy and connected.

And honestly?

Restaurant staff usually know within minutes whether a couple genuinely enjoys being around each other.

Make bathroom checks someone’s actual responsibility during service.

Who checks it? And when?

Watch what happens after a table leaves during your busiest service.

How long before it’s cleared? Who owns it? Does someone walk past it three times before doing anything?

Set the expectation before service, not after you’ve spotted the problem.

Pay attention to the final 30 seconds.

You don’t need some cheesy script. But your team should know that hospitality doesn’t end when the EFTPOS machine comes out.

A thank you. Eye contact. Remembering their name. “Hope we see you again.”

Small things.

The little things are usually the first things to disappear when a restaurant gets busy.

caption:
Okay, so how do you actually fix these?

The Mistake: Empower your team to come to you with a solution, not hide the problem. “I screwed this up. I know how to fix it. I’m on it — just keeping you in the loop.” Mistakes get much bigger when staff are too scared to tell you they’ve made one.

The Menu Question: At your next pre-shift, pick ONE dish or drink and ask everyone to describe it without reading the menu. You’ll learn a lot.

The Handoff: Make passing on the important information part of the standard. The allergy. The birthday. The missing drink. The problem that’s already been explained.

A guest shouldn’t have to tell their story three times.

These aren’t massive changes. They’re things you can start doing on your next shift.

caption:
Regulars don’t just walk into a restaurant.

They walk into a relationship that’s been built over dozens of visits, hundreds of conversations and thousands of tiny moments.

After more than 20 years of owning and operating restaurants, here are 12 things I notice that most guests never see…

1. Someone spots them before they’ve even reached the door.

2. The smile they get is different. You can’t fake genuine excitement when one of your favourite regulars walks in.

3. Their favourite drink is already on someone’s mind before they’ve even sat down.

4. The conversation doesn’t start from scratch. It picks up exactly where it left off last time.

5. Other regulars notice they’ve arrived too. Great restaurants quietly build communities.

6. The newest staff member is usually the last one to learn who they are.

7. Great regulars never expect special treatment. That’s often why they end up getting it.

8. The team remembers the little things. Their usual table. Their favourite wine. The fact they hate coriander.

caption:
I notice great servers almost immediately.

Not because they can carry four plates.

Not because they know the menu by heart.

3. They seem to know exactly when to approach the table… and, more importantly, when not to.

7. They recommend their favourites because they’re genuinely excited for you to enjoy them, not because they’re trying to increase the bill.

8. They never make you feel awkward for asking a question, changing your mind or needing another minute.

9. You’d never know they’re in the weeds. Somehow, they make chaos look calm.

10. They leave little moments behind that have nothing to do with the food. A joke. Remembering your name. A perfectly timed comment. Those are the things people talk about afterwards.

11. They don’t look like they’re performing hospitality. It just feels like who they are.

12. And my favourite… they’re not afraid to have a little fun. If they spot a camera, they’ll smile, wave or jump into the moment instead of pretending it isn’t there. Those tiny, genuine interactions are often what people remember most.

alt: Video by Hospitality Advisor ┃Alexis Guttridge on July 15, 2026.

caption:
One of the most interesting parts of consulting is this…

Restaurant owners usually know something doesn’t feel right. They just don’t always know what’s causing it.

They bring me in to fix one thing… but after a few hours on the floor, we’re often talking about something completely different.

Here are seven conversations I have all the time…

1. “I think it’s a staffing problem.” Most of the time, it’s actually a leadership and communication problem.

2. “We need more customers.” Sometimes. But more often, we need to give the customers you already have a better reason to come back.

3. “Our service is inconsistent.” Service usually isn’t the problem. Training and clear expectations are.

4. “Guests just aren’t spending enough.” Often they would… if the team felt more confident making recommendations.

5. “We’re flat out all the time.” Being busy and being efficient are two very different things.

6. “People keep leaving.” Before we blame pay, I always want to understand what it’s actually like to work there.

7. “I think we need to change everything.” Honestly… most restaurants don’t. They need someone to connect the dots they’ve stopped seeing.

If you’ve ever said one of these, which one was it?

caption:
One of my favorite things about spending most of my life in restaurants?

Regulars.

Not because they spend the most money.

Not because they know the menu.

Because over time, something really special happens.

People stop being customers.

And start becoming part of the story.

Here’s what I’ve noticed.

1. The best regulars aren’t usually the loudest.

2. Great regulars know people’s names.

3. They almost always have a favorite table.

4. They bring the people they love to “their place” and act weirdly proud about it.

5. The staff usually know their drink before they sit down.

6. They don’t expect special treatment.

7. They appreciate being recognized, but they never demand it.

8. The really good ones ask staff about their lives.

9. Sometimes they come for the food. Sometimes they come because they don’t want to eat at home.

10. They notice when someone on the team is missing.

11. Staff genuinely worry when they haven’t seen a regular for a while.

12. Some regulars become friends.

13. Some become family.

14. They celebrate birthdays, anniversaries and milestones in the same place year after year.

15. They have stories with the staff that nobody else understands.

16. Restaurants grieve regulars when they’re gone.

17. And after all these years, I’ve learned something.

People think regulars come back because of the food.

But most of the time, they come back because of how they feel when they walk through the door.

And honestly?

That’s the whole game🧡

Regulars…

11. If I can’t picture myself having a Manhattan at the hotel bar, something’s missing. There is just something special about a great hotel bar.

Louder than necessary. Very aware of who’s watching. They want to be seen more than they want to be present.

2. Who’s uncomfortable.

They over-explain, fidget, laugh a beat too late. Something feels off for them tonight.

3. Who’s actually in charge.

Not who’s talking the most. Watch who everyone looks at before they commit to a decision.

4. Who’s lying.

Their words and their body are having two different conversations. Nervous energy they can’t quite contain. They’re managing you, not talking to you.

5. Who’s already checked out.

Phone face up. Half answers. Eyes drifting. Physically present, completely gone.

Once you start seeing it, you can’t unsee it.

Did I miss one?

What’s the biggest tell people reveal before they say a word? ↓

alt: Video by Hospitality Advisor ┃Alexis Guttridge on June 07, 2026.

caption:
I have a soft spot for people sitting alone.

Always have.

Maybe it’s because I’ve spent most of my life in restaurants.

Maybe it’s because I genuinely enjoy my own company.

Or maybe it’s because some of the most interesting conversations I’ve ever had started with a table for one.

Here’s what I’ve noticed.

1. Some of the happiest people in the room came alone. After all these years, I’ve learned that a table for one isn’t nearly as sad as people think.

2. People sitting alone usually have better conversations with staff than people sitting at tables of six. Maybe it’s because they’re paying attention.

3. They order exactly what they want. No negotiating. No splitting. No “I don’t mind, you choose.” Just what they feel like eating.

4. They notice more. The music. The bartender. The couple on their first date. The regular sitting three stools down.

5. Most people aren’t judging them. Everyone’s too busy worrying about themselves.

6. They’re often far more comfortable than people expect. In fact, some of the most confident people I’ve met were sitting by themselves.

7. Some people are travelling. Some are killing time. Some just didn’t feel like cooking. There’s usually a story.

8. A lot of people sitting alone are really interesting. Over the years I’ve met readers, travellers, business owners and some incredible people sitting by themselves.

9. Some people come alone because they genuinely enjoy their own company. And honestly, I think that’s a bit of a superpower.

10. I have a soft spot for tables of one. I usually end up checking on them one extra time and having a little chat if they’re up for it.

11. A table for one doesn’t make me sad. It makes me curious. I’ve had some of my favourite conversations with people sitting alone.

12. And sometimes they are lonely. Sometimes they’ve lost someone. Sometimes they’re figuring out life again. Sometimes they just don’t want to sit at home. And after all these years, I’ve learned that a little kindness and a few extra minutes can mean more than you’ll ever know.

And honestly?

Table-for-one people…

I’d love to hear your stories🧡

caption:
Do you have a favourite restaurant…

…but deep down you know something feels off?

As a former Boston restaurateur, these are usually the first signs I notice that a restaurant is struggling operationally long before the food becomes the issue.

1. Staff look scared to make decisions without approval. You’ll see them checking with management over tiny things they should already feel confident handling.

2. Nobody acknowledges guests walking in. Even a quick “Hey guys, we’ll be right with you” completely changes how welcomed people feel.

3. One employee is visibly carrying the entire shift. You can usually spot them within minutes because they’re quietly fixing everyone else’s mistakes.

4. Tables sit uncleared while staff avoid eye contact with them. Guests start feeling ignored long before anyone complains.

5. The room feels tense instead of busy. Great restaurants can be absolutely slammed and still somehow feel calm.

6. Staff stop helping each other once pressure hits. That’s usually culture breaking down in real time.

7. Guests start looking around confused instead of relaxed. Once uncertainty enters the room, hospitality disappears fast.

And honestly?

Before destroying a small business in a review…

tell the owner first.

A lot of owner-operators care far more than you realize, and sometimes they genuinely have no idea what’s happening once service pressure hits.

caption:
This isn’t just restaurants.

It’s Hotels. Wineries. Bars.

Once you’ve spent enough years creating experiences, you stop walking into spaces the way everyone else does.

You notice things.

Here are 12 things I notice before I’ve even looked at the menu ↓

1. The room.

Before I sit down, I’m taking in the entire space.
The bar.The kitchen.The lighting.The flow.
I’m trying to figure out what story this place is telling.

2. The greeting.

Not whether somebody says hello.
How they say hello.
You can learn a lot about a business in the first ten seconds.

3. The sound.

Not the music.
The room.
Can I hear the person sitting across from me?
Or am I about to spend the next two hours yelling over dinner?

4. Manager A

If I see a manager running food, clearing a table, seating guests or helping the team, I immediately relax.
The best managers I’ve ever worked with were never too important to do the work.

5. The staff.

I watch how they communicate.
The best teams feel connected.
The worst teams feel like everyone is fighting their own battle.

6. The energy.

Restaurants should feel like controlled chaos.
Guests should never feel the chaos part.

7. The water glass.

Please don’t hand me a water glass that’s still hot from the dishwasher.
I’d genuinely rather wait.

8. The wine glasses.

Water spots drive me absolutely insane.

9. The cutlery.

I know this sounds ridiculous.
I don’t care.
Good cutlery changes the experience.

10. The table nobody wants.

There’s always one.
Too close to the bathroom.Too close to the front door.

Or my personal favourite...
The genius who puts a high-top table next to a standard-height table so somebody spends the entire meal staring directly at another person’s ass.
*Once you see it, you can’t unsee it.

11. Manager B.

If the restaurant is busy and the manager is parked on a laptop, my eye starts twitching.
You cannot lead hospitality from behind a screen.

12. The menu.

Before I read a single item, I’m looking at the menu itself.
Is it clean?Simple?Intentional?

Now I’m curious.

Hospitality people and guests...

What do YOU notice first when you walk into a restaurant? ↓

caption:
🛟Save this. You’ll use it more than you think.

Here’s what I look for the second I walk in:

1. Who’s performing. Louder than necessary, very aware of who’s watching. They want to be seen more than they want to be present.

2. Who’s uncomfortable. They over-explain, fidget, laugh a beat too late. Something’s off for them tonight.

3. Who’s actually in charge. Not who’s talking the most. Watch who the table checks in with before they commit to anything.

4. Who’s lying. Their words and their body are having two different conversations. Eyes moving everywhere, nervous energy they can’t quite contain. They’re managing you, not talking to you.

5. Who’s already checked out. Still sitting there, phone face up, half answers, eyes drifting. Physically present, completely gone.

Once you start seeing it you can’t stop.

Use it in hiring. Use it in negotiations. Use it when something feels wrong but you can’t explain why.

Trust what you’re reading. 

The room is always telling you the truth.

caption:
When I first met my husband, it drove him nuts to eat out with me.

I notice everything.

Who greets you at the door.
Who makes eye contact.
Who pretends not to see you standing there.

Eventually we made a deal.

If we’re out for fun, I sit with my back to the host stand.

Because those first few seconds can honestly break my heart.

Someone walks in excited to be there.

And sometimes they’re left standing… waiting… unsure if anyone even noticed.

It’s such a small moment.

But it sets the tone for everything that follows.

Food matters.
Atmosphere matters.
But the feeling someone gets when they walk through the door?

That’s the real first course.

And this isn’t just about restaurants.

It’s about business.
It’s about leadership.
It’s about life.

People rarely remember every detail.

But they always remember how you made them feel.

That’s the stuff that actually matters to me.
Watching someone become more solid in their own skin.

If you were in that room, you know who you are.
I’m really proud of you.

caption:
What I’d tell this woman now.

You thought you had to be hard to be respected.
Sharp to be taken seriously.
All edge, no softness.

You believed being “the boss” meant leaving the tender parts of you at the door.

You were wrong. And I say that with so much love.

You don’t lose your drive by becoming softer.
You don’t lose your fire by becoming warmer.
You don’t lose your authority by being human.

The world doesn’t just accept the tough side of you.
It loves the playful side.
The emotional side.
The dog-obsessed, heart-wide-open side too.

It won’t always feel this heavy.
Success won’t always feel like pressure and proving and pushing uphill.

One day it feels spacious.
Grounded.
Earned in a different way.

You’re going to make some brutal decisions. The kind that keep you up at night. And somehow, every single one grows you into a woman you’ll actually like being.

Not just respect. Actually like.

I’m proud of you.
And a little in awe of you, too.

If you’re in your “hard season” right now, keep going. You’re becoming someone you haven’t even met yet.

So I’m making a promise to her. We will find our laughter again. We will stay playful. We will keep living big and open and soft. That’s how she stays with us.

Jed, Axl and I will carry her forward.

We miss you every single day, peanut.

i love you.

His love has made me the happiest I have ever been. 

His love is endless.

caption:
This is me. In all my glory at 40 years old. I have never...⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I have never in my life been so proud of a birthday milestone until this day. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
For many of you who don’t know me on here. I went through many epic life moments both beautiful and very dark the last 15 years to arrive to such a clear and exciting space in life. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I was a drunk. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I was sad and mean. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
To myself and others. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I had hurtful and meaningless relationships time and time again. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I created a business in America that burnt me out so badly I had to walk away from it all. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
But in the courage to walk away I began to smile again, find my healthy self, connect with my amazing and supportive husband, become mum to Axl our 4 legged child who has stolen my heart. And last but not least the creation of PAUSE. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Creating Pause has given me the opportunity to use all of it. The good, the bad and the ugly to help other find balance in the workplace before the burnout happens. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Thank you to all of you that have helped me along this epic life journey. Each interaction. Each hug. Each smile back has made a difference in my life. And I hope to do the same for all of you. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
With love-⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
